claims.text: The initial material is a magnetically soft, relaxed polycrystalline high-entropy alloy with moderate naturally occurring domain-wall pinning.
Severe plastic deformation will introduce a high density of defects into the magnetic high-entropy alloy.
A modest low-temperature anneal will stabilize deformation-induced defect structures.
The low-temperature anneal can stabilize defects without significant grain growth.
Severe plastic deformation will increase dislocation density and create defects such as sub-grain boundaries.
Dislocations and deformation-induced sub-grain boundaries can serve as pinning centers for magnetic domain walls.
The introduced defects create local energy barriers that impede domain-wall motion.
Impeded domain-wall motion requires a higher applied magnetic field to reverse magnetization.
The higher field required for magnetization reversal increases the measured coercive field.
Severe plastic deformation followed by light annealing will produce a notably higher coercive field than the untreated baseline.
The fully annealed untreated baseline has lower coercivity because it contains fewer domain-wall pinning sites.
The coercivity increase should hold only while defect density enhances pinning without causing drastic amorphization or degradation of the magnetic phase.
Excessively high defect concentration may compromise long-range magnetic order.
The predicted coercivity increase is expected under room-temperature processing in argon and room-temperature quasi-static magnetic characterization.
